div.head: EXPLOSION AT DITTON.
div.p: THE EXPLOSION AT DITTON.

On Fri,isy tnerniug last an explosion occurred at Ditton Irenworke, near Viridnes by which raven per- sons lost their 1 v.a. The wcrfcs consist of blasting furnaces, of which there are several, and 'which are in- digenous to Staffordshire and the North of England. The centre furaace contained about twelve or fourteen tons of molten metal ready for manufacturing into "pigs" or pig iron, and ten minutes before the explo- sion took place the foreman and furnace inspector had walked round the furnace an found everything ap- parently all right. Three men were at work in the vicinity of the furnace, while about 40 yards in front of it were seated several men comfortably enjoying their numbing meal. While the men were thus quietly re- freshing themFelves, without the slightest indication a loud explosion was heard, and in a moment, with the rapidity of lightnieg, from the cupola shot forth a huge volume of flame, consuming everything within Its reach. Accompaning it, like a, voleanic eruption, came mclten metal. coke, and ashes, all of a white heat, the destructive elements covering the unfortunate persons who were in front of the furnace. To three persons death was instantaneous' one of them being I little girl named Hill, aged ten years, who had bronglit her father's breakfast, and who was at the time a the accident playing with the sand. The other two were a man named Crawley, aged 65, and ittrick Jeffreys, aged 16, who were working near the furnace. When the bodies of these un- foqnnate man were recovered, the flesh liter- ally fell from their bones while they were being removed. The other persons who have succumbed to the effects of the explosion are—Henry Powell, aged 64; Joseph Hill, 16. brother of the litle girl; John Maddock, 26; and Joseph Bumble? 21. All of them Were frightfully charred and mutilated, the sight they presented being truly sickening. Powell's son was sitting getling his breakfast opposite to another fur- nace, and when the Same had spent its fury he ran to his fat'e's assistance. While tearing from him the burning garments, he himself was severely burnt about the hands. Medical aid was promptly sum- moned, but to alleviate the sufferings of the unfortu- nate survivors was an impossibility. One by one they Succumbed to the effects of thfir injuries within a short time of the accident, and the eighth sufferer, Joseph Hill, the father of the boy and girl who are already numbered with the dead, now lies in a very precarious cendition. The force of the explosion may be imagined when it blew down some stacks of pig Iron 60 yards distant, and carried some of the bars Into an adjoining field some 100 yards away from the pens of the explosion. On visiting the place the day after the explosion, our reporter ob3erved Charred remnants of the Door creatures' clothing lying on the eind beds, and the breakfast cans, which the men had been using, were burned out of shape, Even the ramies clog irons were burned or, and so severe hal been the beat that in some cases the bodies themselves Were literally consumed, .hardly any trace of identifi- Cation remaining. It 13 supposed that the accident has been caused by ccld water coming in contact with the molten metal. The tellege of Ditton is enveloped In complete bloom at the sad occurrence, and great synspathy is felt for the bereaved families.

div.head: TEE INQUEST.
div.p: TEE INQUEST.

Co Monday, at the Blackburn Arms, Ditton, Mr. Drifft.ld, coroner for South-West Lancashire, opened the inquiry into the oircurnstancee attending the deaths of the deceased. The identification of the bodies by the jury was a most sickening process, the remains of the bodies being charred and disfigured in a frightful Manner. The relatives of the deceased persons having proved their identity for the satisfaction of the jury and coroner, an endeavour was made to ascertain if possible the cause of the accident, and for that purpose William Mizell, one of the under managers, was called, Colonel Gamble, of St. Helene, the largest eliarenolder in the concern, being present to watch the proceedings. Dalian said fifteen minutes before the occurrer ce took place. he inspected the furnace and found it working all right. Shortly after eight o'clock when at home getting his breakfast, he heard the ex- plosion, and on going to the works, he found Maddock and others frightfully burnt. The remains of Crawley, Teffreys, and the little girl, Hill, who had come with her father's breakfast, were lying among the red hot metal and cinders which had just belched forth from the furnace. The top had been blown off, and two Courses of brick v. ork had been blown out. He be- lieved the cause of the explosion to have been a leakage from the tnyere. which had let the cold water into the miclten metal. Cold water ran through a pipe into the tuyeres for the purpose of keeping the brickwork and other portions of the furnace cool, or the whole would be consumed from the intense heat. The furnace had worked very steadily and satisfactorily prior to the accident. and it had been put in working order since. —John Powell, the son of one of the deceased. said he was getting his breakfast, as was his father and several others, at the time of the accident. He was some dis- tance away from his father, and he heard a crack, im- mediately follawed by the bursting out of the front of the furnace, earring with it molten metal, ore, and coke, all of s white heat. Be ran for his life, and look- ing back he saw his father in a blaze. The Witness returned to his father, and tried to me him by strip- ping him of his burning garments, burning his hands while he did so. The hodies of the girl. Hill, Crawley, and Jeffreys were " roast'ng " on the pig beds in the hot debris. Be had his father removed and attended to, but he died soon alter.—Thomas Smith, a foundry manager, when asked by the Coroner what was the state of the furnace, replied that he devoted his atten- tion to the dead and dying, and did not lock at the furnace. He succeeded in getting the injuries of the wounded men attended to before the arrival of the doctors. The blast and water were turned off directly after the explosion.—Mr. Percy, the manager of the Wigan Coal and Iron Company's works, who was called at the suggestion of Colonel Gamble, said he had made an examination of the furnace, and from appearance it had been all right prior to the explo•ion. Be believed the canna of the explosion had been the 00 arching" of the furnace, which had caused a sup of the cold material into the mol:en metal, and thus the explosion had been produced. The tuyere must have. been leaking, although he did not think the leakage alone would have done it.—The Coroner said it seemed that if men were working in front of the furnace un- conscious of the danger, it must be very dangerous work.— Mr. Percy s It is dangerons.—The Coroner said It was dangerous to a degree which had not been made apparent before.—The jury, while expressing them- selves satisfied with the evidence of Mr. Percy, desired to have the evidencq of some independent engineer, and the coroner adjourned the inquiry until the 17th Inst. for that purpose.

div.head: FUNEBA.L.
div.p: THE FUNEBA.L.

On Wednesday, the raisins of the victims wan in- terred in Hale churchyard, and in the Roman Catholic burial ground, Appleton. The first funeral that took place was that of John Maddock, a married man, 28 years of age, who was in charge of No. 6 furnace at the very time when the terrible eruption occurred. The procession started at half-past ten o'clock from ' the house, one of a group of small cottages adjacent to the Dittou Junction railway station, and Mr. ' Thornburn the managing director of the corn. pany, kindly placed his private carriage at the dia. posal of the relatives and friends of the deceased. Amongst those who followed the hearse to the grave at Hale were Mrs. Maddock, the widow ; the father, mother, sisters, and other relatives of the deceased; and there were also present Mr. Thornburn, jun., Mr. Thomas Smith, manager of the foundry; and Mr. Ciardiner, cashier of the works. The interment was conducted with quietness, and there was no demon- titration of wild grief on the part of the women, though the appearance of the widow and two orphan children excited great emotion in the spectators. At one o'clock the bodies of Joseph Hill, aged 13, and be Hill, 10, brother and sister, were removed from the dwelling of their unfortunate father and buried in Hale churchyard. As the remains were borne from the house a hymn was sung bye number of the chil- dren connected with the Wesleyan Sunday school, of which the deceased were regular attend:tate. The father of the Hills, who was shockingly burnt by the explosion, lies in a prostrate condition. Independent of his own sufferings on the present occasion, this man has undergone a series of domestic ain ctions which can scarcely lind a parallel, even in the annals of the poor. About sixteen months ago he lost two daugh- tare, the death of whom it is supposed caused their mother to die of a broken heart within two months after, The accident of Friday, besides placing his own life in jeopardy, killed two more of his children, and, as if to crown the bitterness of his situation, the rest of his family. are lying around him suffering from fever. The remains of Henry Powell (uncle to the Hills). and Joseph Plumley, were afterwards buried at Hale, whilst Jan es Crawley. and Patrick Jailers, were in- terred in the Roman Catholic burial-ground, in Apple- ton. two miles from Ditton. To the writer of these lines there was a strain of sadness, though not of sorrow, in the "Auld Lang Syne " with which the members of the Reform (flub greeted Mr. Bright's appearance on Monday evening, There was much of pathos in the idea of the singing— I had almost written, in the fact that the song should have been necessary at all. Without seeking to record the spindrift of history, it is not to be gzinsayed that John Bright and Manchester have beeen "two folks" for well nigh twenty years. The strong metropolis of the Midlands opened her arms for the strong man dis- armed in Manchester, and the tie between them will now probably have only one dissolution. After hear- ing Ur. Bright's platform addresses for the last thirty years, I was curious to ascertain on Monday, after an Interval of some eight or nine, how the well-known voice would ring. I got into an embrasure on the right of the platform, and waited, out of sight of the orator, for his opening sentences. Spoken as they were, amidst an almost solemn hush on the part of the audience, with great deliberation and deep feeling, the familiar syllables smote upon my ear with all the charm of old days. Of all conspicuous public men that I have ever eeen or heard, or ever known in tale or history, none—save the friend of his bosom, who rests amidst the swelling downs of Sussex—ever had half the sense of solid sincerity for me which, from the first day I heard him to the last, seemed to inform the public utterances of John Bright. The feeling of awe deepened sometines into one of fear of him as of a smiting prophet. Even after one got to know him in what I may call the Paulton days of the old Examiner, when pleasant tea-drinkings twioe a week were now and then honoured with the presence of the then mem- ber for Manchester—it was diffioult to away with the trepidation of which I speak. And once more, on Monday, I found the old senC- ment coming uppermost. Unlike all other speaking, it seemed like a dividing asunder of things—it had no peer, it was not to be imitated—the voice, the pose, the manner, the collocation of language, t' e similes, the broad but lambent Minion., the denunciation swelling to its close like an Ocean billow breaking upon a shore, have, in my judgment, no parallel in any past or pre- sent masters of our English tongue. Presumably, over the long period of which lam treating, there must have been certain changes in Mr. Bright's speak- ing •' but to me it has always been the same. To say that he has been educating himself during that period is no doubt true enough, simply because, if he had not done it himself, he would have dodged the only pos- sible tutor fit for the task. John Bright's oratory is John Bright himself—himself and none beside. I remember that in dear old " Pinnook " it is re- marked of William the Conqueror, thaa "there was not a man of that day who could bend his bow or handle his arms." And the same in a different sense may be said of the oratory of the Member for Birmingham. The rush and sweep of Gladstone are like the scimitar of Saladin—the onslaught of Bright seems made with the battle-axe of Crear de Lion. Amongst living speakers there is none like unto him, no not one. It was to Mr. Huskisson, I believe, that the Duke of Wel- lington said when the Right Hon. Henry had resigned, owing to a mistake: "There was no mistake, there is no mistake, and there shall be no mistake, Right Hon, Henry, be pleased to pat that into your meerschaum, and pull away!" Now, in John Bright's speeches, their remarkable directness and unmistakableness can be appreciated by political babes; they are as easily digested as a cottage loaf administered in level slices— there are no lumpy bite to stick in the throat and inter- fere with the easy absorption of the diet; you never have to go back upon a sentence so as to miss the nest and get pat out; all is plain sailing; there are no big words of foreign extraction—moustachioed and ear- ringed like thou of which Mr. Sheil was so fond—the word-drink is from the pure well of English undefiled. The ordinarily accepted notions of oratory, as we used to get them in school books and from professors, are utterly upset when John Bright—as the Irish say— "takes the flare." Demosthenes and his celebrated pabulum of pebbles sink into a manufactured myth, and savour of quackery. John Bright is a law in this matter to himself; he knows what he means, and he imp what he means; there is and there shall be no mistake. He has a central fire of oonviotion, and it mutt be expressed outwardly; and it must be com- municated and it is communicated and light Sashes back from the audience upon the speaker' and both are warmed. When people tell you that they have been "carried away" by somebody's eloquence, you may be quite sure that they have not been carried far. Similarly, when women tell you they have been " riveted " by a preacher, the expression is all lip ser- vice. John Bright neither carries you away nor rivets you. He does not smooth you down or oil you, or adminieter sweet syllabubs or lullabies, or any such thing. He makes you possess your souls and your senses in peace, only olearing the smiles from your eyes and the brushwood of prescription from your tree trunks.

And so on Monday we sat in the embrasure at the Reform Club and listened, after many days. to the old voice—mellowed, not impaired, by the /dun fur anal. We thought what a strong and yet what a tender soul that voice represented. Who ever speaks of old Melds like that speaker P Great heart how the molten kind- ness drops from it upon The place beneath. We sit in the embrasure and think of to-day—of the voice of to- day and of the same voice at Durharo—and then of the long spell between Durham and Windsor, when the chief of the State acknowledged the services of a lifetime, and herself paid tribute to one of the fore- most of her subjects. Old voice, old times! In lis- tening to that voice we seemed to return to the shady elms by the lanes of our fathers—where they prayed and where they rest, and the grand familiar notes of the "Old Hundredth" stream out into the quiet air as they did long ago, before, like wandering sheep we strayed or had to be brought to the fold again.

div.head: ANOTHER WIFE'S EYE DESTROYED.
div.p: ANOTHER WIFE'S EYE DESTROYED.

Another wife has had an eye destroyed besides the poor creature who was lately so savagely assaulted by her husband at Warrington. A frightful assault was committed in Sheffield on Friday night by a brick- layer, named James Id‘Donald, who attacked his wife. and destroyed her eye with a kick; then beat her cruelly and drove her into the streets half naked, where she was found covered with blood and nearly dead. On Saturday the prisoner was sent to gaol for six months, and ordered to keep the peace for the fol• lowing ex months.

M. ILLINOWORTH ON LORD DERBY. At the meeting addreesed by Mr. Forster, 'MX., at Bradford on Saturday, Mr. Illingworth, who was re- ceived with great cheering, said that while Mr. Thomp. ion justly expressed confidence in Lord Derby, be would remind him that Lord Derby was not the entire of her Majesty's Government, and more than that, nu- fortunately, he was not its head—(cheers) —and further, that the nobleman who was now. at its head was by no means the puppet of his own Government. However much they might admire Lord Derby's heart and the lines upon which he had gone—for be was more a Radical than anything else—it was unfortu- nate that he had hardly the confidence of kis own con- victions, and he seemed to be very like charles the Second, who never said a foolish thing and never did a wise one. (Laughter and cheers.)

A LICENSING COMMITTEE AND THE GROCERS.

A resolution was adopted at a meeting of the County Licensing Committee at Lancaster, on Satur- day, urging that such an alteration should be made in the law as would rest in the justices the power to grant or refuse grocers's licenses and Itemises to sill intoxi- cating liquors off the premises.
FATAL OCCURRENCE TO A FATHER AND CHILD.

Mr. E. C. Pearson, chemist, Bradford, was on Satur- day discovered by his wife lying dead on his bedroom floor. The body of his son, aged four years, was found underneath the corpse. It is believed that deceased was seized by an apopletic fit and fell on his son, who was thus suffocated.

div.head: SOCIAL SCIENCE AT LIVERPOOL.
div.p: SOCIAL SCIENCE AT LIVERPOOL.

The twentieth annual congress of the Social Science A; a niation was opened on Wednesday night in Liver- pool. The first general meeting was held in tbe Philharmonic Hall, when Lord Aberdare resigned the President's chair to the Marquis of Huntley, who delivered a lengthy address, which was mainly devoted to the education question.
THE "REPEA.L " MEMBER FOR WESTMEATH.

Mr. P. J. Smyth, the "Repeal" member for West. meath, has incurred the displeasure of the Roman Catholic clergy for separating himself from Mr. Butt and the Home Bale party. A ranting of a portion of the clergy of the diocese which has been held, presided over by Bishop Nulty, passed a resolution declaiiog that Mr. Smyth "had forfeited the confidence of the people and the clergy." This will be generally re- garded as equivalent to a "notice to quit."

div.head: HOW FEVER IS PROPAGATED.
div.p: HOW FEVER IS PROPAGATED.

A serious outbreak of typhoid fever has occurred at Padetow, Cornwall, where, in a population of some 2,000 persona, 200 have been struck down with fever, It appears that a system of drainage has been con• struoted, chiefly at the expense of the lord of the soil, Mr. Prideaux Benne, but during the summer months there was not sufficient water to carry the matter out of the drains, where it lay till the heavy rains stirred it up, with the result of poisoning 10 per cent, of the population. There have, as yet, been only four deaths, so that the fever has appeared in a mill form.

div.head: NORTH OF ENGLAND IRON TRADE. THE BATE OF WOB.
div.p: NORTH OF ENGLAND IRON TRADE. THE BATE OF WOB.

On the part of the employers' representatives of the North of England manufactured iron trade, notice of a termination a the present rate of wages at the end of the year, with a view to a reduction has been given. The present wages, Ss. 3.1. per ton, is the lowest tbst has prevailed for more than ten years, except for a short period when 85. was paid. The men are now very dissatisfied, and will take badly to a further re- duction, even though trade generally is so depressed. At a meeting of the Board of Ai bitration, representing the northern ironwork, held at Darlington on Mon- day, an important question was considered. In llsy last some of the workmen of ironworks at Stockton struck agiinst the wages for manufacturing light rails whioh had been fixed by Mr. Rupert Kettle, arbitrator. The men resisted every entreaty, even of their fellow. operatives, to return t 3 their employment. Other men were obtained, and the firm incurred a lose, they state, of £6OO, which they now claim through the Board. This question was considered at some length, but the Board failing to come to any understanding, it was adjourned.

div.head: CONGREGATIONAL UNION.
div.p: THE CONGREGATIONAL UNION.

The autumnal meeting of the Congregational Union commenced on Tuesday, at Bradford. The President (Rev. Dr. Aveling) delivered an address in which the Eastern Q testion found a prominent place. Reference ta the "new fledged Earl" provoked much laughter, which was changed to enthusiastic applause when the reverend President described Mr. Gladstone as "Eng- land's true spokesman." Resolutions on the educa- tion question and intemperance were passed. Among other subjects with which the President dealt were Ritualism, the Established Church, the Burial Laws, Communion with other Churches, and National Edu- cation. A resolution was afterwards passed appoist- ing a committee ti inquire and report as to the best method of meeting the evils resulting from intem- perance.

At the Congregational Union, on Wednesday, a re. solution was carried by acclamation declaring that the conduct of the English Government, and especially of the Prime Alinister, in relation to the atiocities re. neatly committed in Bulgaria, has created just indi- gnation and alarm, and affirming that no settlement of the relations between the Porte and its agents in the East of Europe can be permanently satisfactory that does not grant to the provinces Complete administra- tive independence. It was also resolved that the Assembly Bhould tender its congratulations to the Presbyterian Church of England, which was lately formed by the union of the two leading Presbyterian Churches in this country.

SETTLEMZNT OF THE MARKET QUESTION. The Cnereatille read a letter from Mr. Hall, Lord Stamford's agent, stating that his offer of the land in B, haw's-lane, for a Market site was still open, and as he had several applications for the land, at a higher Pries than that offered by the Board. he wished the taatter settled. If the Board took the plot there would be no objection on the past of Lord Stamford to allow It year or two so elapse before the Board erected the Market holm, and when that was done he would sell to them the Market tolls for the amount stipulated, a thousand pounds. Mr. Bunoess. after referring to the discussion at the kat meeting, when the voting on the question of a Market, was equal, he said, to that of the four who 'toted against the resolution, two could hardly be ex- Pected to do otherwise, seeing that they had spent a Rood portion of their lives in places of business on either side of the present market place and to vote in favour of the resolution proposed would seem to them to vote against their own interests and the interests of their chief friends, (Cries of chair.) Mr. BIUMM.—You are not entitled to make aline Sion to motives. ' The Crum:Kam—l think it is scarcely parliamentary to impute motives. Mr. Btniartes.—l am not without hope that the fentlemey alluded to, with a fuller consideration of the question and the exercise of a little self-denial, will be induced either to support the resolution or decline to Oppose it. Mr. Thennerr.—You are imputing motives to them, Which I think is ye. y unfair, Mr. Burgess. Mr. BYROM.—Our only motive was to get a market Place at as small a cost as possible. , Mr. BTSR4EB9.—One of the gentlemen alluded to said he did not care where the market was taken to. [klr. Byrom: No more be does.] Referring to the supposed annoyance to the patients in the Dispensary if the market were in Shaw's-lane, be said that the proposed Cite was at the opposite end of the geld, and a consider. "Me distance from the Dispensary. After a somewhat sharp dispute, between the Chair- Man and Mr. Burgess, as to whether the latter gentle- man was in order, Mr. Browns proceeded to state that one of the two objectors said that it was prema- ture to decide upon that particular spot, and if they Waited a few years it was probable that a better site Would be offered, and one in the direction of the pro- posed new railway station was suggested' but it could tearcely be considered premature to settle a question that had been before this Board for two years, during Which time Mr. Kinsey had been a member; and as to the new railway station, they had not very much to do With that ; but what little they had he hoped would be done in facilitating rather than frustrating the accom- plishment of that flinch-needed improvement. Last, but not least. Mr. Timperley asked if anything had been said in the candidatee' addresses about the mar- ket. It might not be needed to answer that question further than to say that it is not very wise to attach ,too much importance to election addresses, for they all knew how much easier it was to make promises than It was to keep them, and they also knew how very soon Come men seem to forget their obligation to their own friends, and would even turn their backs upon them When they had got all they could out of them. In Conclusion, he said, I hope the Board will vote in favour of the resolution and in harmony with the true interests of the ratepayers, and if they do so we may reasonably hope that the ratepayers will ratify the ver- dict when their turn comes. I move that the plot of Land situate in Bowdon-road, and containing 2,620 yards, be purchased for the purpose of a market, the price not to exceed 4d. per yard. (Rear, hear.) Mr. Cows= seconded the motion, and said that he believed that a good Market and Corn Exchange would Improve the trade of Altrincham, and be a great bene- fit to the town generally. Mr. BYROM said that he was not going to offer any personal remarks lest he hurled back the false insinua- tions that had been thrown out Sy Mr. Burgess. His object in speaking upon that question had been, not to keep the market near his shop, but simply to secure a Market that would meet the requirements of the town at a small cost as possible and so keep down the rates. It never had been with him a question of taking the market from his own shop, or of establishing it Close to anybody, else's place of business. He merely Wished to do what he considered was the beet for the Interests of the ratepayers. He was afraid that if the resolution was adopted and carried into effect it would be the means of saddling the ratepayers with largely increased rates. He thought that if they waited a short time they might be able to obtain a more central mite than the one proposed, and one that would be more convenient for the kwhole town. Under those Circumstances he moved, as an amendment, that the market question be adjourned time die. (Hear, hear.) Mr. NJ:um, in second,ing the amendment, said that in his opinion the propond site was not sufficient cen- tral, and that if the matter was deferred for a year or tWo—and there was nothing particularly urgent about It that he was aware of—more eligible sites might pre. lent themselves to them. Mr. BURGESS said that if the question was left over for a few years it was probable a better site might be offered, and that in his opinion the probabilities were in an entirely different direction. The Board then divided, with the following result: For the amendment, 6—Messrs. Byrom, Kinsey, Tim- perley, Smith, Beishaw, and Berratt ; for the original motion, 4—Xesers. Burgess, Cowsill, Ambler, and Neoyon. The Crair.XAN declared the amendment carried. - This concluded the businees.

CHARGED WITH ASSAULTING A
GIRL.

joseph Pulkner,e well-known blacksmith of Altrin- oham, was charged, at the Altrincham Pollee Oonrt, on Friday, before Mr. Norris, with an assault op m Ellen Gillibrand, aged 14, at Altrinoham, on the 6th instant.

The girl stated that she was just turned 14 years of. age. On Thursday morning, about ten o'clock, she was in her mother's shop at Goose Green, Altrinoham • when prisoner came and asked if her mother was In. Witness was not aware that she was out, and said she thought she was in the back kitchen. Prisoner then osme inside behind the counter, where she was stand- ing, and eat down on a chair. In a minute or two after be threw her down on the floor. She screamed and called fer lobr mother. At that moment her mother came in at the door. Her mother had a portion of a bans in her hand, and with that ehe struck at prisoner and knocked him over on the floor. saying" What are you doing there, you villain f" Prisoner said "No- thing," and began to abuse her mother. Her mother then took the poker and struck him once or twice, and pushed him out of the house. The prisoner was not sober at the time. . . . . .

Harry Wainwright Bellhonse stated that he was in Gillibrand's shop when the prisoner cams in., He said "Hellos, little bookkeeper, is your mother in ?" and the girl replied "I think she is in the bask kitchen." Prisoner then commenced pulling her hair and " rollocking " with her, and witness left. He met the moth er about 20 or 30 yards away, and told her she was wvited. Sarah Gillibrand, the girl's mother, stated that she went out of the house by the baok door, leaving her daughter, who did not know she had left the house, in the shop. She met the prisoner at the corner, and he spoke to her, but she did not recollect what he said, nor did she reply to him. She was away about ten minutee, and on her return met the last witness (Bellhouse), who told her that she was wanted. She then hurried back, and when within three or four yards of the front door she heard her daughter screaming. She went in and asked him what he was doing there. He replied that he was doing nothing, and called her bad names. She got the poker and struck him, and pushed him out of the house. _ .

P.C. Harrington apprehended the prisoner on war- rant on Friday afternoon, when, in reply to the charge, he denied the assault, and said .All that I did was to tap her on the shoulder and rollock with her a bit." . .

The prisoner said there was not the slightest shadow of truth in the charge. It was done for spite, arid, he had never heard such &mass of perjury committed in his life. Mr. Norris said the case was proved to his satisfac- tion, and he had no option but to commit him for trial at the sessions. Bail would be accepted, himself in £5O and two sureties in £25 each. The bail was forthcoming, and the prisoner Was liberated.

At the Altrincham Patty Sessions, on Monday, That, Parker Stanbank, James Robinson, and George Pres- cott, were summoned for being drunk and refusing to quit the licensed premises of John Hunt, at Bowdon, on the 4th of October last.—Mr. Atkinson appeared for the.def once. Mr. Hunt stated that he kept the Griffin Inn, and on the 4th inst., at about a quarter to ten at night, he saw the three defendants on his premises. There had been a disturbance, and a bust ornament of Shakespeare had been broken. He desired the defen- dants to go out, but they did not seem inclined. They wanted something to drink, soda water, but he refused to serve them.—George Rawlinson said he was called into the house by Mrs. Hunt, and found it all in an up- roar, the glasses lying under a table, the seats wrong side up, and an ornament broken. There was no fighting then. In reply to the Bench, witness said that Stanbank was inclined t 3 fight. Prescott was walking about with a pocket bask wanting to have the names of parties, as Mr. Hunt would not supoly them with anything. Robieson was trying to get Stanbank away —ln reply to the Bench, Mr. Hunt said that the defen- dants would not leave at his request. Mr. Atkinson said that these gentlemen were going home from market, and they called there. He did not think it was any part of his duty to say that they were not a little "fresh." There was no doubt some little dis- turbance did take place, but after they were soled to go out, according to Mr. Hunt's evidence, they did not say they would not go, and.it was quite evident that Robinson was doing\ his bast to take the party out against whom there might appear to be any ground for saying he was quarrelling. As gentlemen, if they did anything wrong, they tendered their apologies to the Bench and to Mr. Hunt. If everyone behaved as Mr. Hunt had done in preventing quarrelling, the magistrates would not have as much business as they had had that day. The Chairman said the magistrates were very much obliged to Mr. Hunt for bringing this case forward, inasmuch as they wished te give every support to those landlords who tried to conduct their houses decently and reepeotably. There was no doubt from the evidence that these three persons were guilty of . refusing to leave the house. The mere fact that they did not utter a verbal refusal was not needful. They would be fined 20s and costs each, or in default one months' imprisonment. The flues were paid.

div.head: LECIURE AT BOWDON ON POLITICAL ECONOMY.
div.p: LECIURE AT BOWDON ON POLITICAL ECONOMY.

The Rev. W. Cunningham, who has been engaged by the Bowdon Literary and Scientific Society, to give a course of lectures on Pol.tioal Economy, delivered the first a the series on Friday night, in the Parish Church Schoolrooms, Bowdon.

Mr. CIINNINGIUX, expressed regret that a good deal of prejtidice was due to mistakes about the meaning of the term political economy. They were rather in- clined to dislike economy, and to think that the science Was a sort of cheeeepaling thing. The common idea was that it was the science of keeping the poor alive with the least possible amount of food. (Rear, hear, and laughter.) It was an entirely false and wrong idea, for economy was just the Greek word for house- keeping. It told us about the arrangements of a house, and how to make the best use of what we have, so as to get the most comfort, the most convenience that was possible from our means. The correspondence be- tween domestic and political economy in this respect was to be considered. Domestic economy could not tell us the best sort of comfort to have in our houses, but only how to get the kind of comfort which we choose' and in this way economy had not got to do with the means of living, but rather with the end which we choose to set before ourselves. It was true in re- gard to political economy —in regard to what he might call the housekeeping of the State. For, just as different people had different ideas of comfort and convenience in household arrangements, so different nations had different ideas of prosperity for a State. Political economy was the science which, assuming the facts of human nature and of the physical world, considered the laws of the production and the distribution of wealth. The laws of political economy expressed the forms ac- cording to which the force of self-interest manifested itself. They told us what would take place in all cir- cumstances where self-interest was uncontrolled, and also what had a tendency to occur in any society of human beings. Political economy had been styled by Carlyle 'a dismal science," and by others as a kind of Morrison's pill which would put the world perfectly right, (Laughter.) He had not much hope that the world would be put right by this simple science. Poli- tical economy had not such a high mission before it, and after all it only dealt with what tended to happen and not by any means; with what ought to happen. The two main divisions which he should be able t go over before Christmas were the production and distribution of wealth—the getting of wealth, and the dividing of it.
At the conclusion of the lecture, which was listened to attentively throughout, a vote of thanks was ac• corded the lecturer on the motion of Canon Gore.

Mr. Starkey Smith, surgeon, de- posed that he made a post-mortem examination- of the body, which was that of a full-grown female child, on Friday morning. It appeared to have been in the water a frrtnight or three weeks. There were no ex• ternal marks of violence which could be seen. A piece of blue braid was round its neck, tied in a single knot. Oa opening the body be failed to find any, evidence of respiration. Except in the braid round the neck, there was nothing to indicate that violence had been used, and the rtite fibs heart went to contradict the idea of strangulation, and he therefore thought it might be safely considered to have been a still-born child, as the lungs had never been inflated. A lORY NEWSPAPER ON MR. GLADSTONE.

Tem saying that no man is a hero to his valet was explained by Goethe, who said that it was not because the hero is not a hero but because the valet is a valet. The gentlemen's gentlemen, who are engaged by Tory newspapers in the present crisis, to dance attendance upon Liberal statesmen, to follow them from public meeting to public meeting, and to deliver to us their letters in the must gracious manner they can com- mand, follow the example of their fellow- 1 flunkeys in the fashionable world, and re- lieve their feelings, in the intervals of service, by abusing their superiors to their hearts' content. Conspicuous amongst this unhappy class arer the writers of a news- paper to which Mr. Bright did the honour of referring, in half a dozen contemptuous words, in his recent speech The Manchester Courier represents that large section of the Tory party which, bringing to the science of . politics neither independence of thought, acquaintance with facts, nor the literary art which may do much to disguise these dis- qualifications, disarms the serious criticism of political opponents, and only offends one by taste. You cannot enter into a contro- versy with a person who tacitly admits the' he is but the mouthpiece of the opinions of others, that he is obeying the summons of the wether-bell to the best of his ability; 1 but you can c&uarrel with him if, in the dis- charge of this humble office, he commits I unpardonable offences of vulgarity and in- decorum, exceeding all the bounds of pos- sible social intercourse. A man may be a fool and a gentleman at the same time; but a- fool who is coarse, ribald, and also a knave, forfeits even the silent contempt of decent people, and society is bound to whip him now and then to encourage the others. The Courier of last Wednesday containe I two leading articles on Mr. Gladstone, which, looked upon as specimens of English journalism, and considering the language in which they are written, the spirit which animates them, and the reasoning which they attempt, are simply disloyal and dishonourable to the English Press, to which the paper presumes to belong. Those of Mr. Gladstone's bitterest opponents, who are also men of fairness and judgment, deny him neither genius, patriotism, nor noble aims. They may say that he is irritable and impulsive, they may be hostile towards him in proportion to the very success with which he carries out a policy to which they are opposed, and-in the heat of political con- troversy, they may sometimes assail his character, instead of assailing his opinions. Mr. Bright told us that the difference betwe ,3n the two great parties is, that during the last twenty years the Liberal leaders have learned something, and that the Tory leaders have learned nothing. if there are appa- rent contradictions in the public career of Mr. Glaistone, these apparent contradic- tions are in reality the singular consistency of a great mind, which adapts itself with an exquisite sympathy to the ever-changing conditions of national life. The most sig- nificant proof of Mr. Gladstone's influence is brought to us every day by his enemies, the impotent rage and resistance which he has the gift of provoking, is the best evidence we could have of a corresponding amount of sympathy and support. But there is a difference between the roar of an infuriated lion and the piteous howls of a whelp, and the spectacle of the Manchester Courier wor- rying Mr. Gladstone is not less ludicrous than that of a gnat trying to stiug an elephant. - On Monday evening a great meeting of working men was held in London, and the principal resolution carried was to the effect —"That this meeting, accepting the admis- sion of the Prime Minister that the policy of the Foreign Office is not in accordance with the public sentiment, demands the im- mediate assembly of Parliament, that the national will may find constitutional expres- sion. And, further, this meeting, and the great majority of the people of England, re- garding the present crisis as one requiring statesmanship characterised by boldness combined with prudence, earnestly appeals to the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone to re- sume the active position he formerly occu- pied in the House of 015mmons, and to undertake to find a suitable mode of expres- sion for the wishes of the people by a policy in harmony with the will of the nation." A long and eloquent letter was read from Mr. Gladstone, which contained a marvellously lucid statement of the present aspect of the Eastern difficulty in its relation to the conflict- ing interests of the Great Powers, "But," Mr. Wacistone writes, "the question has also a domestic atct of serious and growing importance. The r7:1110 Minister has ad- mitted that his views of Eastera policy are not those of the people Yet the Government will not, it seems, by a dissolution allow the people an opportunity of expressing their sentiments in an authen- tic manner." Mr. Gladstone then urges continued agitation for an autumn session, and concludes with the words—" It is a duty to strengthen the hands of a Govern- ment when disposed to do good; but I know of no duty to strengthen them for evil." It seems as if this challenge, nulling the kennele of the Manchester Courier, the leash of the two youngest cubs was slipped, and if their bite does not hurt much, their bark, as we shall see, reflects credit upon their female parentage. It might be supposed that if Mr. Gladstone is committing political suicide by " rendering himself ridiculous in the eyes of Europe by the display of blind and , passionate vanity," that this course would [ be encouraged by opponents who desire the extinction of his p3wer. But this is not the ungenerous view which the Courier takes. The spectacle is a painful one, and poetic justice will not be fulfilled, if Mr. Glad- stone disgraces himself by persisting ss", dissolution which would upset the present Government, and thus rob the poet of the future of the idyllic subject of "Disraeli and Gladstone" dividing the spoils of office in a quiet, gentlemanlike, way. On Wednesday ,it was stated that the Servian Government has resolved to accept a 0' regular " armistice so soon as proposals in due form shall have been submitted to it by the representatives of the Great Powers. Concurrency with this announcement there are further charges against the Turks of having committed atrocious cruelties in Servis. The grounds on which the Grand Council at Constantinople resolved to grant an armistice for six months are stated in a telegram. The Council foresees serious military disadvantages if only a short suspension of arms were granted, and it hopes also to be able to make progress with the peace negotiations during the winter.

On Thursday the public were informed that the ob- ject of the Turkish Government in proposing a six months' armistice is explained in a telegram from Constantinople. Believing that a cessation of hostili- ties for six weeks would be attended with danger in the event of the peace negociatione leading to no satis- factory result, the Extraordinary Council resolved on the more extended period on the ground that it would enable the Porte in the interval to calm the fanatichro of the Mussultrian population, would obviate the risk of being compelled to resume hostilities when the in- clemec,cy of the season might render operations more difficult, and would offer facilities for coming to an understanding on the condition 4 of peace and the re. forms to be introduced into the Empire. A Belgrade telegram says the Bervian Minister for Foreign Affairs has received reports from various pre- fects of fresh ads of barbarity on the part of the rutkish troops. They are said to have wantonly massacred and burned old men, women, and children. Some corpses have been found without arras, ears, and tongues, and others with their heads cut off and dis- embowelled,

With regard to actual warfare, it is said that Idukhtar Padua is apparently getting the worst of it in the contest which he himself renewed. Duko vies, with seven battalions of troops, is reported to have turned his positions, burnt Ljubinie, and defeated the troops sent from Stolatz to relieve the town, while Bukovitch, with 4,000 men, is marching to intercept the reinforcements sent to the aid of the Turkish com- mander from ostar.

div.head: LORD DERBY'S DESPATCHES.
div.p: LORD DERBY'S DESPATCHES.

The despatch forwarded by Lord Derby to Sir Henry Elliot on the subject of the outrages in But. garia was published on Saturday morning. It states that the general arming of the Mussulman population on the order of the Vail of Adrianople led to the assemblage of bands of murderers and robbers, who, under pretext of suppressing insurrection, were guilty of the most heinous crimes of the present century. Not only was the meat culpable apathy displayed by the great majority of the provincial authorities in allowing or conniving ut such exoesses, but little or nothing effeetual his bean dons in the way of repara- tion. The auth,rity of the Porte was set at defiance, and the Government at Constantinople kept in igno-. ranee of the truth. Under no other circumstances could the Porte have been led to promote and deco- rate officials whose acts have been at ewe a disgrace and an injury to the Turkish Empire. Sir Henry Elliot is in=tructed to seek a personal audience of the Sultan, to demand reparation and justiee to the in- jured people; that the persons who have been deco- rated or promoted under a false view of their conduct shall be tried and degraded; that the eighty women taken from their homes shall be restored to them; and, in order to fully restore public confidence, that the disturbed districts shall at once be placed under an able and energetic Commissioner, who, if not himself a Christian should have Christian coml. cellars in whom the Christian population would repose trust.

div.head: MARQUIS OF BATH.
div.p: THE MARQUIS OF BATH.

At the annual matting of the Westminster Farmers' Club, on Friday, the Marquis of Bath, replying to the toast of his health, said he bad but little to add to, and nothing to detract from, ,what he said at Promo the other day. With the opinions there eZpressed he was prepared to abide. He denied that ,the agitation was °riginally set going for patty Purposee, but ,admitted that it had of late been made use of in that way, one of the reasons being the idiotic aoudad of the Conser- vative press, more particularly the Globe and Standard, in which the most fulsome articles appeared. They had been told that they ougnt to be silent upon a mat- ter of this kind, but he maintained that it was the duty of every Englishman to express his opinion upon the policy of the Government. A. full expression of that opinion could not do otherwise than strengthen its hands. As to I.tust.i.a, he believed the Ministers of that country were anxious not to go to war, and if England and Russia were only united he could not see the pos- sibility of a European war. England and Russia united had the power of averting such a contingency. rJr himself, he wanted to see a perfect understandingbe- tween England and Russia on the matter.

MR. FORSTER, M.P., ON THE TURKISH ATROCITIES.

Mr. Forster addressed a great meeting of bis con. etituents at Bradford on Saturday. He expressed his surprise at the tone of the speeches delivered by some members of the Ministry since Parliament rose, and regretted that Lord Derby's despatcb, which was pub. lisle(' on Saturday, had not been sent weeks before. The outrages had not yet ceased, and notwithstanding the language of the deep etch, he doubted whether any real compensation would be given to the victims, the chief cffenders punished, or the Turkish population disarmed. The right hon. gentleman statekunliesita-. tingly that there had been no exaggeration whatever in the accounts which had been published concerning the Tiiikish atrocites, criticised the language of the Prime Minister at Aylesbury, reviewed the foreign policy of the Administration as applied to the Eastern Question, and pointed out that Lord Derby's great ob. ect ought to be to cling to joint scion on the part of the six Powers. The meeting he addressed increased his conviction that this was one of those cases which the people of England had takento heart, and that they had come to the conclusion that it was a matter in which the fulfilment of England's duty was the beat protection for English interests.

The author of a pamphlet on this subject has re ceived from Mr. Gladstone the following letter : " Gervaux Abbey, Dedale, Oct. 6, 1876. Sir,— I am very glad that you are about to draw public attention to the relation of the Jews to the Eastern Question, as I do not doubt from the tone of your letter that you will treat the subject in the in. tenet of justice.

I have always had occasion to admire the conduct of the English Jews in the discharge of their civil duties, but I deeply deplore the manner in which what I may call Judako sympathies beyond as well as within the oircle of professed Judaism are now acting on the question of the ist, while lam aware that as regards the Jews themselves there may be much to account for it. In any event I think they certainly ought to have the benefit of those principles of civil E quality which, unless the convictions and desires of this nation are to fail of effect, will I trust be established in the provinces now forming the chief objects of public attention. With every good wish I remain, sir, your faithful i servant, W. E. GLADETONE. L. Glackstein, Esq."

div.p: MR. GLADSTONE'S LETLER.

An important letter from Mr. Gladstone was read at a meeting in London on Monday night on the Eastern Question. The right hon. gentleman reviews the course of events and the policy of the Government in eo far as it has been disclosed in blue-books and speeches, and accuses them of wilfully, persisting in a policy which has dean emphatically condemned by the nation. The people of England have determined that in so far as in them lies the people of Bosnia, Herze- govina, and Bulgaria should enjoy the blessings of self-government. If Lords Derby and Beaconsfield would demand those terms from the Forte they would put an end to the controversy at home ; but Mr. Gladstone can find no trace of such a resoleition. He has been charged with attacking the Administra- tion, but he can find no obligation to strengthen the hands of a Goveinment that is doing evil. Finally, the right hon, gentleman declares that his store of hope is exhausted, and he calls upon the country to compel the Administration to respect its will. A vigorous contribution to the discussion of the question was made on Monday night at Hawick by Mr. G. 0. Trevellyan, M.P.
